179v0ff:458: Benchmark gaming is essentially a Principal-Agent Problem: model providers have strong incentives to optimize metrics that are easy to measure, rather than capabilities that are truly valuable to users. The core tension revealed by this Anthropic blog post is that the systematic gap between evaluation environments (hardware, sampling strategies, test set splits) and real deployment environments is often larger than the differences between models themselves. The finding that "3x is a watershed" points to a deeper fact: as model scale increases, GPU memory bandwidth, inference throughput, and context length become more important bottlenecks than model architecture. In evaluation environments, these factors are deliberately controlled or optimized; in actual production environments, long contexts, high concurrency, and multi-turn conversations quickly expose the gap. A few percentage points of score difference can be completely drowned out by engineering factors in real-world scenarios. The danger of reducing benchmark scores to a single factor is that it creates a "Capability Illusion" — a model performing well on a specific benchmark does not mean its performance is uniformly strong across the task space. Historically, both AlphaGo in the domain of Go and the BERT era went through similar phases of "surpassing human benchmarks but performing mediocrely on real-world tasks."
